Adam argues the authorization is massive in absolute terms but represents only about 4% of current market cap, a modest figure. tts_summary: This morning's note is a focused intraday piece — no broad macro color, just a deep dive on Nvidia's freshly announced buyback expansion. Here's what you need to know. Nvidia said it is boosting its repurchase authorization by an additional one hundred fifty billion dollars, taking the total program to two hundred thirty-five billion dollars. The company expects to exhaust that authorization through fiscal year twenty-twenty-eight, so we're talking roughly one and a half years of execution. Management framed it as a confidence statement in the long-term opportunity ahead. Now here's Adam's take, and it's important: on the surface this sounds massive, and in absolute dollar terms it is. But two hundred thirty-five billion is only about four percent of Nvidia's current market cap. That is not a dramatic figure when you put it in context. Adam draws a comparison to Apple back in twenty-thirteen, when an aggressive capital return program coincided with material multiple expansion. Some bulls are leaning on that analogy to argue Nvidia is at a similar inflection point. Adam pushes back on two fronts. First, Apple's multiple expansion in that era was driven more by the market waking up to the services business — think App Store fees — than by buybacks alone, even though buybacks helped at the margin. Second, and more importantly, Apple carried a far larger cash pile as a percentage of its market cap in twenty-thirteen than Nvidia does today. The situations are not directly comparable. The deeper issue is this: the primary reasons Nvidia trades at a depressed multiple right now are concerns about the sustainability of the AI spending boom, rising competitive pressure, circular financing activity, and growing balance sheet liabilities. None of those issues get resolved by today's buyback announcement. Until those structural concerns are addressed, the headline authorization number — however eye-catching — is unlikely to be the catalyst that unlocks a sustained re-rating. Bottom line: mixed reaction is the right framing. The buyback is a positive signal on management confidence and will provide a technical floor over time, but it does not change the fundamental debate around Nvidia's core overhangs. Watch how the stock trades on this news as a real-time sentiment read.
